A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SIS/NACC graph-quantification work. Their text, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–D were included in the comparison.

before.justification: Section 4, Figure 2, and Table 1 report original quantification experiments on five graph datasets under unshifted and synthetically shifted conditions.

after.justification: Sections 4.2–4.3 and Appendices B and D report original benchmark, Twitch, kernel-sensitivity, and feature-kernel comparison results.

M1.justification: SIS changes from approximating importance weights using only test-density KDE in v1 Equation 13 to separately estimating training and test densities for their ratio in v2 Equation 12. v2 also introduces interpolation between PPR and a constant kernel. These change the central weighting procedure, although the reported experiments use a constant training kernel. NACC's one-hop construction remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 retains the five citation/co-purchase datasets and adds Twitch Gamers, estimating explicit-content-streamer prevalence within five language communities under natural distribution shift. It also adds random-walk-induced structural shifts. The unshifted evaluation shown in v1 Figure 2 is no longer reported.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds the previously published Ego-network Quantification method, represented by EgoNet with PACC, and evaluates its SIS/NACC extensions. Appendix D additionally compares structural SIS against feature-only importance sampling. MLPE and the standard count baselines remain; the existing shortest-path comparison moves to Appendix B.

E3.justification: v2 adds Twitch's training and language-partition evaluation design and random-walk sampling with length 10 and teleportation parameter 0.1. It drops KLD, retaining AE and RAE. SIS now uses interpolation weight 0.9, while the shortest-path decay parameter changes from 0.5 to 3. The original five-dataset split proportions and neural-network sizes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix B substantially extends the existing kernel comparison with PPR-interpolation and shortest-path-decay sensitivity sweeps. Appendix D adds a structural-versus-feature-kernel ablation. These examine kernel choice and sensitivity beyond v1's fixed-setting comparisons. Conversely, v1's classifier-accuracy-versus-quantification-error plot is removed.

E5.justification: The retained benchmark protocol still uses ten splits, ten classifier trainings per split, and the same 95th-percentile one-sided t-test. Both versions omit numerical standard errors from tables and leave plotted shaded bands statistically undefined. v2 explains the omission of standard errors but introduces no new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds Twitch, random-walk, EgoNet, sensitivity, and feature-kernel results while removing KLD and the old unshifted/hard-classifier plot results. Retained entries also change: PubMed MLP-PACC under PPS changes from AE/RAE 0.0311/0.1071 to 0.0181/0.0649 in Table 1, without an explanation. SIS results additionally reflect revised kernel settings and therefore do not establish same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: New Appendix C develops computational-complexity analyses for SIS, dense/sparse PPR computation, shortest-path kernels, and NACC. It includes an optimizer-iteration assumption and contrasts the stated ACC and NACC complexity bounds. v1 contains no corresponding runtime analysis. Most probability-notation changes in Sections 2–3 restate existing mathematics.

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit claim that SIS is the first quantification method to tackle covariate shift systematically, whereas v1 principally emphasizes first classifier-based graph quantification. The two headline contributions—SIS for covariate shift and NACC for class identifiability—and their general effectiveness claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 attributes CiteSeer's poor PPR performance broadly to kernel mismatch. Appendix B supplies a more specific explanation involving disconnected components, small effective samples, and interpolation. It also relates PPR weighting to GNN prediction similarity. Section 4.3 adds qualifications about weaker real-world benefits and classifier dependence, while Appendix D discusses feature-kernel applicability and efficiency.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds a code-repository link, a pointer to versioned dependencies, software libraries and licenses, and CPU/GPU/RAM specifications absent from v1. Appendix C documents dense PPR computation, sparse pruning for Twitch, and GPU shortest-path computation. These materially expand reproducibility information without establishing that previously undocumented implementation choices changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds Milli et al.'s social-network quantification work and explicitly relates ENQ to neighborhood classification plus ACC. It also adds sources for Twitch, PyTorch Geometric, and sparse graph computation. The broader literature framing remains largely intact, and the first-classifier-based-work wording is not reconciled with the newly acknowledged ENQ predecessor.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the introduction, ACC explanation, and NACC discussion are retained. v2 makes targeted language and notation revisions, separates synthetic and real-world result discussions, and moves shortest-path discussion into the new appendix structure. Citation style and author/header presentation also change.

P2.justification: v2 removes the large classifier-accuracy comparison figure, adds a Twitch visualization and two kernel-sensitivity figures, and substantially restructures Table 1. Tables 2–4 provide new displays, including the relocated and revised shortest-path comparison. The conference template also changes text width, headers, typography, and page layout.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's support for its methods: it adds a natural-shift study, evaluates an existing graph-quantification method, investigates kernel failures and sensitivity, and supplies substantial implementation information. These additions improve empirical credibility, applicability assessment, and reproducibility. Unexplained PubMed revisions and novelty wording inconsistent with the ENQ discussion remain weaknesses, but they do not outweigh the substantial gains.
